findings.title: Client removal fails with UnsupportedOperationException when V1 and V2 fine-grained-authz features are both enabled
findings.body: AdminPermissions.registerListener now gates the ClientRemovedEvent handler only on Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (the V1 flag), which can be enabled at the same time as ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. When both are on, the listener calls AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false); management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, clients() returns the new ClientPermissionsV2, and setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). The exception propagates out of the event listener during session.clients().removeClient(...), so deleting any client — and by extension deleting a realm, which removes its clients — returns a 500. The same landmine exists for isPermissionsEnabled/resource/getPermissions. Either make the V2 overrides graceful no-ops for these legacy management methods, or make the listener skip when the V2 feature is active.

findings.title: Missing null check and no migration for the new Clients resource/scopes on existing realms
findings.body: In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no per-client resource exists the code loads the 'Clients' type resource via AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...) and immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking for null. getResourceTypeResource returns null whenever the admin-permissions resource server was initialized before this change: AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns early when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() already exists, so realms that already had FGAP v2 enabled never get the new 'Clients' resource or the new scopes (configure, map-roles, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite). For such realms every client admin operation that reaches this fallback throws an NPE (500), and creating any Clients-typed permission fails with 'Scope does not exist'. Add a null check here (mirroring the no-arg hasPermission) and provide an upgrade path that adds the new schema objects to existing admin-permissions resource servers.

findings.title: canMapRoles/canMapCompositeRoles/canMapClientScopeRoles ignore manage permission and MANAGE_CLIENTS role
findings.body: These three methods only evaluate the explicit map-roles* scopes and, unlike canManage/canView in the same class, do not short-circuit on root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS) and do not treat a manage permission as implying map-roles. This is inconsistent with the rest of the class (canConfigure and canView both chain through canManage) and with UserPermissionsV2, where manage transitively grants map-roles (asserted by testTransitiveUserPermissions). Consequence: under V2, an admin holding the manage-clients role, or a manage permission on a specific client or on all clients, gets 403 when mapping client roles to users or adding composite roles — a regression compared to V1 behavior, where manage clients implied the ability to map its roles.

findings.title: getResourceName does not resolve names for Clients-typed resources
findings.body: getResourceName only special-cases the Users resource type, resolving the stored user id to the username. For the newly added Clients resource type it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is never set for FGAP-created resources (getOrCreateResource only sets name/scopes), so admin REST responses and the admin console will show a null/empty name for client-typed permission resources instead of the client's clientId. Add a Clients branch mirroring the Users one that resolves ClientModel.getClientId().

findings.title: Javadoc on void require methods incorrectly says "Returns {@code true}"
findings.body: The newly added javadoc for requireView() ("Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}.") and requireViewClientScopes() ("Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}.") describes a boolean return, but both methods are void and throw ForbiddenException on failure. This contradicts the otherwise consistent 'Throws ForbiddenException if ...' wording used for the other require* methods and misleads implementers of the interface.
